title: Miniature bowl (part of a dollhouse set)

altText: A tiny glass bowl shown close up against a plain background, with a simple rounded shape. It is a miniature made for a dollhouse.

context: A tiny glass bowl made in the early 19th century as part of a dollhouse set. The Met's object page gives its size as about 1 by 1.9 centimeters (3/8 by 3/4 inch), smaller than a coin, and lists its culture as German.

descriptions.k: This tiny bowl is made of glass. It is made for a dollhouse. It is smaller than a coin! Look at its round shape. Who could use a bowl this small? What would you put in it?
descriptions.g12: This is a bowl made for a dollhouse. It is made of glass and is only about two centimeters wide, smaller than most coins. People made it long ago, in the early 1800s. Look at its curved shape. What does it tell you about how small things can still be carefully made?
descriptions.g35: This bowl is only about 1 centimeter tall and 1.9 centimeters wide, smaller than a coin. It was made of glass in the early 1800s as part of a dollhouse set, with other tiny cups and dishes. Even though it is a toy-sized object, its shape is clear and smooth. Why would a maker go to so much trouble to make such small things?
descriptions.g68: Miniature household objects like this glass bowl let children and adults play with a tiny version of home life. At about 1 by 1.9 centimeters, it was made in the early nineteenth century as part of a dollhouse set, probably with matching cups and dishes. Making glass this small requires control and patience. What does a miniature copy of an ordinary object tell us about what people valued in daily life?
descriptions.g910: This glass bowl from a dollhouse set, made in the early nineteenth century, reduces an everyday vessel to the size of a fingertip. The smallness shifts our attention to its shape and transparency, and it invites us to imagine the larger world it belongs to. Dollhouse objects could be toys, teaching tools, or collectors' items, though the record does not say which. Consider how scale changes the meaning of a simple form.
descriptions.g1112: As a miniature, this glass bowl exists between toy and model. Made in the early nineteenth century as part of a dollhouse set, it replicates a domestic form while exaggerating its fragility and perfection through scale. The Met's record does not tell us who owned it or how it was used, so claims about play, education, or display must be tentative. How do miniatures turn ordinary objects into subjects for contemplation, and what do they reveal about the domestic life they imitate?

teacherNote.context: A tiny glass bowl, about 1 by 1.9 cm, from an early nineteenth-century dollhouse set. The Met lists the culture as German on its object page. Which dollhouse the set belonged to is not stated in the record.
directions: Have students measure out 1 by 1.9 centimeters on a ruler and discuss how small the bowl really is.
Ask students to design a miniature object from their own home and explain what must stay the same for it to be recognizable.
Discuss whether miniatures are toys, models, or art, and invite multiple viewpoints.
